title: How to set prices
summary: Prices come from combining the cost study, competitors' prices and your commercial judgment.

sections.heading: Profit as one more cost
paragraphs: Many entrepreneurs see profit as "what's left over". The handbook proposes the opposite: include the desired profit as one more cost, before deciding to open. If with that profit prices are comparable with the competition, the project is viable; if they're well above, it must be reworked or dropped.

What profit is reasonable? More than the money would earn in a government bond or a term deposit, because opening a business means risk and work. At least twice the yield of a three-year government bond.

sections.heading: The theoretical price
paragraphs: Net price = standard unit cost × coefficient, where the coefficient spreads the other costs and the desired profit over the raw materials.
Taxes and fees on sales are added to the net price to get the menu price.

sections.heading: From theoretical price to real price
items: If your price is well below the market, you can raise it.
If it's similar, don't change it much.
If it's well above, consider taking the product off the menu.
Neither the "rule of 3" nor copying competitors guarantees recovering the investment.
